sections.title: Design Forces and Deformations
sections.summary: Calculate QUD and QUF per the Section 3-2.11.2-3-2.11.5 procedures.
sections.body: [p. 49] Calculate the deformation-controlled actions QUD, and force-controlled actions QUF, accordance with the linear analysis procedures of Sections 3-2.11.2 to 3-2.11.5.
key_points: Pure procedural cross-reference
sections.applicability: Bridges the LSP load/modeling procedure to the acceptance criteria.

sections.title: Component and Element Acceptance Criteria
sections.summary: Deformation-controlled: Phi*m*QCE >= QUD (Equation 3-13); force-controlled: Phi*QCL >= QUF (Equation 3-14); BOTH primary and secondary components must be checked.
sections.body: [p. 49] Components and elements analyzed using the linear procedures of Section 3-2.11.2 to 3-2.11.5 shall satisfy the requirements of this section. Prior to selecting component acceptance criteria, classify components as primary or secondary, and classify actions as deformation-controlled or force-controlled, as defined in Section 3-2.5. 3-2.11.7.1 Deformation Controlled Actions. For deformation-controlled actions in all primary and secondary components, check that: Φ m QCE ≥ QUD Equation (3-13) where QUD = Deformation-controlled action, from Linear Static model m = Component or element demand modifier (m-factor) as defined in Chapters 4 to 8 of this document. Φ = Strength reduction factor from the appropriate material specific code. QCE = Expected strength of the component or element for deformation-controlled actions. QCE, the expected strength, shall be determined by considering all coexisting actions on the component under the design loading condition by procedures specified in ASCE 41 Chapters 9 through 12. Note that this includes interaction equations for shear, axial force, and moment and that these equations include force- and deformation-controlled actions, as well as expected and lower bound strengths. Use the appropriate resistance factor for each action, as specified in the material specific design codes (i.e., the Φ factors in ACI 318, the AISC Steel Construction Manual, etc). 3-2.11.7.2 Force-Controlled Actions. For force-controlled actions in all primary and secondary components: Φ QCL ≥ QUF Equation (3-14) where QUF = Force-controlled action, from Linear Static model QCL = Lower-bound strength of a component or element [p. 50] for force-controlled actions Φ = Strength reduction factor from the appropriate material specific code. QCL, the lower-bound strength, shall be determined by considering all coexisting actions on the component under the design loading condition by procedures specified in ASCE 41 Chapters 9 through 12. Use the appropriate resistance factor for each action, as specified in the material specific design codes (i.e., the Φ factors in ACI 318, the AISC Steel Construction Manual, etc). 3-2.11.7.3 Secondary Elements and Components. All secondary components and elements must be checked to ensure that they meet the acceptance criteria. Deformation-controlled actions are checked according to Equation 3-13 and force-controlled actions are checked according to Equation 3-14.

Equation 3-14: Phi*QCL >= QUF

sections.title: Nonlinear Static Procedure
sections.summary: NSP has no DCR or irregularity limits (3-2.12.1); a 3D model with optional secondary components (3-2.12.2); stability must be considered (3-2.12.3); one load case with the Table 3-5 dynamic increase factor (3-2.12.4, 3-2.12.5); acceptance by expected deformation capacities and Equation 3-17 (3-2.12.6, 3-2.12.7).
sections.body: [p. 50] The NSP and limitations to its use are provided in the following sub-sections.

sections.summary: No DCR or geometric irregularity limitations apply.

sections.title: Analytical Modeling
sections.summary: 3D model of primary elements (secondary optional but must be checked post-hoc if omitted); explicit force-displacement response (incl. strength degradation/residual strength) discretized along each member; explicit connection modeling required if weaker/less-ductile or if flexibility changes forces/deformations by >10%.
sections.body: [p. 50] To model, analyze, and evaluate a building, employ a three-dimensional assembly of elements and components. Two-dimensional models are not permitted. Create one model, as shown in Figures 3-13 and 3-14 for either framed or load-bearing wall structures, respectively. Inclusion of secondary components in the model is optional. However, if the secondary components are omitted, they must be checked after the analysis, against the allowable deformation-controlled criteria (e.g., to check the connections of gravity beams in a steel structure, compute the chord rotation and compare against the allowable plastic rotation angle for that connection). Include the stiffness and resistance of primary components. Note that the strength reduction factors are applied to the nonlinear strength models of the deformation controlled components (e.g., the nominal flexural strength of a beam or connection is multiplied by the appropriate Φ factor). Analyze the model for the Nonlinear Static load case defined in Section 3-2.12.4 Use the stiffness requirements of ASCE 41 Chapters 9 through 12 to create the model. Discretize the load-deformation response of each component along its length to identify locations of inelastic action. The force-displacement behavior of all components shall be explicitly modeled, including strength degradation and residual strength, if any. Model a connection explicitly if the connection is weaker or has less ductility than the connected components, or the flexibility of the connection results in a change in the connection forces or deformations greater than 10%. [p. 51] If the building contains sections that are less than three stories and are attached to the sections with three or more stories, the designer shall use engineering judgment to include some or all of the shorter section if there is any possibility that the presence of the short section will affect the taller section in a negative manner.

Explicit connection modeling required beyond a 10% force/deformation-change threshold

sections.body: [p. 51] Live load reduction is allowed, if the requirements in Section 3-2.3 are met. 3-2.12.4.1 Loads. To calculate the deformation-controlled and force-controlled actions, simultaneously apply the following combination of gravity loads: Increased Gravity Loads for Floor Areas Above Removed Column or Wall. Apply the following increased gravity load combination to those bays immediately adjacent to the removed element and at all floors above the removed element; see Figures 3-13 and 3-14: GN = ΩN [1.2 D + (0.5 L or 0.2 S)] Equation (3-15) where GN = Increased gravity loads for Nonlinear Static Analysis D = Dead load including façade loads (lb/ft2 or kN/m2) L = Live load including live load reduction per Section 3-2.3 (lb/ft2 or kN/m2) S = Snow load (lb/ft2 or kN/m2) ΩN = Dynamic increase factor for calculating deformation-controlled and force-controlled actions for Nonlinear Static analysis, use appropriate value for framed or load-bearing wall structures. see Section 3-2.12.5 Gravity Loads for Floor Areas Away From Removed Column or Wall. Apply the following gravity load combination to those bays not loaded with GN; see Figures 3-13 and 3-14. G = 1.2 D + (0.5 L or 0.2 S) Equation (3-16) where G = Gravity loads [p. 52] 3-2.12.4.2 Loading Procedure. Apply the loads using a load history that starts at zero and is increased to the final values. Apply at least 10 load steps to reach the total load. The software must be capable of incrementally increasing the load and iteratively reaching convergence before proceeding to the next load increment.

sections.title: Dynamic Increase Factor for NSP
sections.summary: Table 3-5 gives ΩN: steel framed 1.08 + 0.76/(θpra/θy + 0.83), reinforced concrete framed 1.04 + 0.45/(θpra/θy + 0.48), load-bearing walls 2. The smallest θpra/θy of any primary element, component or connection within or touching the increased-load area governs; columns are omitted.
sections.body: [p. 52] The Nonlinear Static dynamic increase factors are provided in Table 3-5. In Table 3-5, θpra is the plastic rotation angle given in the acceptance criteria tables in ASCE 41 and this UFC for the appropriate structural response level (Collapse Prevention or Life Safety, as specified in Chapters 4 to 8 of this UFC) for the particular element, component or connection; θy is the yield rotation. For steel, θy is given in Equation 9-1 in ASCE 41. For reinforced concrete, θy is determined with the effective stiffness values provided in Table 10-5 in ASCE 41. Note that for connections, θy is the yield rotation angle of the structural element that is being connected (beam, slab, etc) and θpra is for the connection (determined from ASCE 41 and this UFC). Columns are omitted from the determination of the DIF. To determine the DIF for the analysis of the entire structure, choose the smallest ratio of θpra/θy for any primary element, component, or connection in the model within or touching the area that is loaded with the increased gravity load, as shown in Figures 3-13 and 3-14. In other words, the DIF for every primary connection, beam, girder, wall element, etc that falls within or touches the perimeter marked as A-B-C-D must be determined and the largest value is used for the analysis. The method behind this procedure is explained in Appendix C. Table 3-5 (Dynamic Increase Factors for Nonlinear Static Analysis), ΩN: Steel, Framed: 1.08 + 0.76/(θpra/θy + 0.83). Reinforced Concrete, Framed: 1.04 + 0.45/(θpra/θy + 0.48). Reinforced Concrete, Load-Bearing Wall: 2. Masonry, Wood and Cold-formed Steel, Load-bearing Wall: 2.

sections.title: Component and Element Acceptance Criteria
sections.summary: Deformation-controlled: expected deformation capacity must exceed the maximum calculated demand (a direct deformation comparison, not an m-factor equation); force-controlled: Phi*QCL >= QUF (Equation 3-17, identical form to Equation 3-14).
sections.body: [p. 53] Components and elements analyzed using the nonlinear procedures of Sections 3-2.12.2 to 3-2.12.5 shall satisfy the requirements of this section. 3-2.12.7.1 Deformation-Controlled Actions. Primary and secondary elements and components shall have expected deformation capacities greater than the maximum calculated deformation demands. Expected deformation capacities shall be determined considering all coexisting forces and deformations in accordance with Chapters 4 to 8 of this document. 3-2.12.7.2 Force-Controlled Actions. For force-controlled actions in all primary and secondary elements and components: Φ QCL ≥ QUF Equation (3-17) where QUF = Force-controlled action, from Nonlinear Static model QCL = Lower-bound strength of a component or element. Φ = Strength reduction factor from the appropriate material specific code. QCL, the lower-bound strength, shall be determined by considering all coexisting actions on the component under the design loading condition by procedures specified in ASCE 41 Chapters 9 through 12. Use the appropriate resistance factor for each action, as specified in the material specific design codes (i.e., the Φ factors in ACI 318, the AISC Steel Construction Manual, etc).
key_points: Deformation-controlled: expected deformation capacities greater than the maximum calculated deformation demands (p. 53)
Force-controlled: Φ QCL >= QUF (Equation 3-17) (p. 53)

equations.description: Phi*QCL >= QUF, force-controlled NSP acceptance (same form as 3-14/3-19)

sections.applicability: The final pass/fail check for every NSP-analyzed component.

sections.title: Nonlinear Dynamic Procedure
sections.summary: NDP has no DCR/irregularity limits (3-2.13.1); full-structure model incl. the to-be-removed element (3-2.13.2); stability must be considered (3-2.13.3); loads applied to equilibrium THEN the element is removed within 1/10 of the vertical response period (3-2.13.4); acceptance via direct deformation comparison and Equation 3-19 (3-2.13.5/3-2.13.6).
sections.body: [p. 53] The NDP and limitations to its use are provided in the following sub-sections.
key_points: Gravity loads are applied to the full model to equilibrium, then the column or wall section is removed (p. 54-55)
sections.applicability: Overview of the NDP sub-sections.

sections.title: Limitations on the Use of NDP
sections.summary: No DCR or geometric irregularity limitations apply.
sections.body: [p. 53] There are no DCR or geometric irregularity limitations on the use of the NDP.
key_points: NDP always usable
sections.applicability: Confirms NDP has no applicability restrictions.

sections.title: Analytical Modeling
sections.summary: Full 3D model of the ENTIRE structure including the element to be removed (unlike LSP/NSP, which model the post-removal condition); same discretization/connection-modeling rules as NSP.
sections.body: [p. 54] To model, analyze, and evaluate a building, employ a three-dimensional assembly of elements and components. Two-dimensional models are not permitted. Create a model of the entire structure, including the wall section and column that are to be removed during the analysis. Include the stiffness and resistance of primary components. Note that the strength reduction factors are applied to the nonlinear strength models of the deformation controlled components (e.g., the nominal flexural strength of a beam or connection is multiplied by the appropriate Φ factor). Inclusion of secondary components in the model is optional. However, if the secondary components are omitted, they must be checked after the analysis, against the allowable deformation-controlled criteria (e.g., to check the connections of gravity beams in a steel structure, compute the chord rotation and compare against the allowable plastic rotation angle for that connection). Apply the loads per the loading procedure in Section 3-2.13.4. Use the stiffness requirements of ASCE 41 Chapters 9 through 12 to create the model. Discretize the load-deformation response of each component along its length to identify locations of inelastic action. The force-displacement behavior of all components shall be explicitly modeled, including strength degradation and residual strength, if any. Model a connection explicitly if the connection is weaker or has less ductility than the connected components, or the flexibility of the connection results in a change in the connection forces or deformations greater than 10%. If the building contains sections that are less than three stories and are attached to the sections with three or more stories, the designer shall use engineering judgment to include some or all of the shorter section if there is any possibility that the presence of the short section will affect the taller section in a negative manner.
key_points: NDP models the FULL structure with the element still present, then removes it during the analysis -- a key distinction from LSP/NSP
sections.applicability: NDP-specific modeling requirement (dynamic removal event).

sections.title: Lateral Stability and P-Delta Effects
sections.summary: Overall vertical/lateral stability and local stability (lateral-torsional buckling) must be considered.
sections.body: [p. 54] Note that overall vertical and lateral stability as well as local stability (i.e., lateral torsional buckling) must be considered.
key_points: Same stability-consideration requirement as NSP
sections.applicability: NDP stability-check requirement.

sections.title: Loading
sections.summary: GND = 1.2D+(0.5L or 0.2S) (Equation 3-18, same form as Equation 3-11/3-16) applied to the ENTIRE structure, monotonically to equilibrium, THEN the column/wall is removed in under 1/10 of the vertical-response period; analysis continues to maximum displacement or one full vertical-motion cycle.
sections.body: [p. 54] Live load reduction is allowed if the requirements in Section 3-2.3 are met. 3-2.13.4.1 Loads. To calculate the deformation-controlled and force-controlled actions, apply the following gravity load per the loading procedure given in Section 3-2.13.4.2: [p. 55] Gravity Loads for Entire Structure. Apply the following gravity load combination to the entire structure. GND = 1.2 D + (0.5 L or 0.2 S) Equation (3-18) where GND = Gravity loads for Nonlinear Dynamic Analysis D = Dead load including façade loads (lb/ft2 or kN/m2) L = Live load including live load reduction per Section 3-2.3 (lb/ft2 or kN/m2) S = Snow load (lb/ft2 or kN/m2) 3-2.13.4.2 Loading Procedure. Starting at zero load, monotonically and proportionately increase the gravity loads to the entire model (i.e., the column or wall section have not been removed yet) until equilibrium is reached. After equilibrium is reached for the framed and load-bearing wall structures, remove the column or wall section. While it is preferable to remove the column or wall section instantaneously, the duration for removal must be less than one tenth of the period associated with the structural response mode for the vertical motion of the bays above the removed column, as determined from the analytical model with the column or wall section removed. The analysis shall continue until the maximum displacement is reached or one cycle of vertical motion occurs at the column or wall section removal location.
key_points: Equation 3-18: identical form to Equations 3-11/3-16
Element removal duration must be <1/10 of the governing vertical-response period
Analysis runs to max displacement or one full vertical-motion cycle

equations.description: GND = 1.2D+(0.5L or 0.2S), gravity load for the entire structure (NDP)

sections.applicability: The NDP loading and dynamic-removal procedure.

sections.title: Design Forces and Deformations
sections.summary: Calculate NDP demands per Sections 3-2.13.2-3-2.13.4.
sections.body: [p. 55] Calculate component design forces and deformations in accordance with the nonlinear analysis procedure of Sections 3-2.13.2 to 3-2.13.4.
key_points: Procedural cross-reference
sections.applicability: Bridges the NDP procedure to acceptance criteria.

sections.title: Component and Element Acceptance Criteria
sections.summary: Deformation-controlled: expected deformation capacity must exceed the maximum calculated demand (same direct comparison as NSP); force-controlled: Phi*QCL >= QUF (Equation 3-19, identical form to Equations 3-14/3-17).

Expected deformation capacities shall be determined considering all coexisting forces and deformations in accordance with Chapters 4 to 8 of this document. [p. 56] 3-2.13.6.2 Force-Controlled Actions. For force-controlled actions in all primary and secondary components, Φ QCL ≥ QUF Equation (3-19) where QUF = Force-controlled action, from Nonlinear Dynamic model QCL = Lower-bound strength of a component or element. Φ = Strength reduction factor from the appropriate material specific code. QCL, the lower-bound strength, shall be determined by considering all coexisting actions on the component under the design loading condition by procedures specified in ASCE 41 Chapters 9 through 12. Use the appropriate resistance factor for each action, as specified in the material specific design codes (i.e., the Φ factors in ACI 318, the AISC Steel Construction Manual, etc).

equations.description: Phi*QCL >= QUF, force-controlled NDP acceptance (same form as 3-14/3-17)

sections.applicability: The final pass/fail check for every NDP-analyzed component.

sections.title: Enhanced Local Resistance
sections.summary: Required for RC II Option 1, RC III, and RC IV; ensures perimeter columns/walls (and their connections) fail in a ductile flexural mechanism rather than a sudden shear failure. ELR is waived if the element was already designed for an owner-approved, risk-assessed design-basis threat.
sections.body: [p. 56] Enhanced Local Resistance (ELR) is required in three cases: RC II Option 1 (Tie Forces and ELR), RC III (Alternate Path and ELR), and RC IV (Tie Forces, Alternate Path and ELR). All three cases contain the same objective, which is to insure that a ductile failure mechanism can form when the column or wall is loaded laterally to failure. To meet this objective, the column or wall must not fail in shear prior to the development of the maximum flexural strength. Two components must meet the ELR requirement: 1. The column or wall, and 2. The connections between the end of the column or wall and the lateral supports (floor slab, base plate, etc). Note that design for ELR is not required if the wall or column has been designed for a specific design basis threat, providing that the design basis threat was developed with a risk assessment approach that was approved by the building owner, government agency or other responsible entity.
key_points: Ductile-flexure-before-shear objective, for both the member and its end connections
Waived if a specific, risk-assessed design-basis threat already governs the element's design
sections.applicability: Overview of the ELR method.

sections.title: Load and Resistance Factor Design for Enhanced Local Resistance
sections.summary: Equation 3-20, Φ Rn >= Ru, with all strength reduction factors Φ = 1.0 and expected material strengths (over-strength factor applied to the lower bound strength) for shear, flexure and all other actions.
sections.body: [p. 56] The LRFD approach is used for ELR design, Φ Rn ≥ Ru Equation (3-20) where Φ Rn = Design strength Φ = Strength reduction factor [p. 57] Rn = Nominal strength, including over-strength factors Ru = Required strength The design strength provided by a component is taken as the product of the strength reduction factor Φ and the nominal strength Rn. For ELR, all strength reduction factors Φ shall be 1.0. In addition, the material strengths for shear, flexure and all other actions shall be the expected material strength (i.e., with the appropriate over-strength factor applied to the lower bound material strength).
key_points: Equation 3-20: Phi*Rn >= Ru, but Phi is always 1.0 for ELR (distinct from Section 3-2's material-code Phi)
Uses expected (not lower-bound) material strength throughout

equations.description: Phi*Rn >= Ru, ELR LRFD check (Phi=1.0)

sections.applicability: The LRFD basis for both flexural and shear ELR demand checks.

sections.title: Flexural Demand
sections.summary: The flexural demand is simply the nominal flexural strength Rn of the column/wall, under the RC-II/III/IV-specific conditions of Sections 3-3.3 through 3-3.5.
sections.body: [p. 57] The flexural demand is the nominal flexural strength (Rn) of a column or wall under the conditions specified in Sections 3-3.3, 3-3.4, and 3-3.5.
key_points: Flexural demand = the column/wall's OWN nominal capacity (not an externally applied load)
sections.applicability: Sets up the shear-demand calculation in Section 3-3.1.2.

sections.title: Shear Demand
sections.summary: The shear demand is the required shear strength to achieve the flexural demand (formation of a three-hinge mechanism or similar), considering effects that increase the nominal flexural strength and never less than with zero axial load; determined out-of-plane, in both directions at corner and re-entrant corner columns. Examples are in Appendices D and E.
sections.body: [p. 57] The shear demand is the required shear strength (Ru) of the column or wall that is necessary to achieve the required flexural demand of the component, i.e. at the formation of a three-hinge mechanism or similar failure mode in the component. In calculating the shear demand, consider any effects (axial load, end conditions, etc) that may act to increase the nominal flexural strength; in no case shall the shear demand be less than that of the column or wall with zero axial load acting. Include any applicable material over-strength factors. The shear demand shall be determined for the horizontal out-of-plane direction (i.e., perpendicular to the building perimeter façade). Columns at building corners or re-entrant corners shall be evaluated in both directions normal to the building perimeter façade. Examples of this procedure are provided in Appendices D and E.
key_points: Shear demand = required shear strength to achieve the flexural demand, at a three-hinge mechanism or similar failure mode (p. 57)
In no case less than that of the column or wall with zero axial load acting (p. 57)
Determined for the horizontal out-of-plane direction; corner and re-entrant corner columns in both directions (p. 57)
Examples of the procedure are provided in Appendices D and E (p. 57)
sections.applicability: The shear-demand calculation feeding the Equation 3-20 check.

sections.title: ELR Location and Extent Requirements
sections.summary: RC II Opt 1: corner + penultimate first-story columns/walls; RC III and RC IV: ALL first-story perimeter columns/walls. One-way wall buildings apply ELR to the FULL end wall and penultimate wall length in every case.
sections.body: [p. 57] 3-3.2.1 RC II Option 1. For RC II Option 1 and framed and two-way load-bearing wall buildings, ELR is applied to the perimeter corner and penultimate columns and load-bearing walls of the first story above grade. For one-way load-bearing wall buildings, ELR shall be applied to the entire length of the end wall and penultimate wall; it is recognized that the majority of the penultimate wall may be interior to the structure, but it must still be designed for ELR. 3-3.2.2 RC III. For RC III and framed and two-way load-bearing wall buildings, ELR is applied to all perimeter columns and load-bearing walls of the first story above grade. For one-way load-bearing wall buildings, ELR shall be applied to the entire length of the end wall and penultimate wall; it is recognized that the majority of the penultimate wall may be interior to the structure, but it must still be designed for ELR. [p. 58] 3-3.2.3 RC IV. For RC IV and framed and two-way load-bearing wall buildings, ELR is applied to all perimeter columns and load-bearing walls of the first story above grade. For one-way load-bearing wall buildings, ELR shall be applied to the entire length of the end wall and penultimate wall; it is recognized that the majority of the penultimate wall may be interior to the structure, but it must still be designed for ELR.
key_points: RC II Opt 1: corner + penultimate only
RC III / RC IV: ALL first-story perimeter elements
One-way wall buildings: always the FULL end + penultimate wall length, regardless of RC

equations.description: ELR location requirement by Risk Category

sections.applicability: Determines which specific elements need an ELR check.

sections.title: RC II Option 1 Shear and Flexural Requirements
sections.summary: Flexural demand = the as-designed nominal flexural strength (no modification needed); shear demand is derived from it via Section 3-3.1.2, with iterative re-checking if increasing shear capacity itself raises the flexural demand.
sections.body: [p. 58] For RC II Option 1, the flexural demand for the columns and walls is the nominal flexural strength (Rn) of the existing or as-designed structure and, therefore, no design modification is needed to meet the flexural requirement. The shear demand is based on the flexural demand of the component as described above. Apply the procedure in Section 3-3.1.2 to the columns and walls to determine the shear demand. If Equation 3-20 is not satisfied, modify the column or wall design such that adequate design shear strength (Φ Rn) is achieved. If the flexural demand is increased as a result of meeting the shear requirement, check that the design shear strength still exceeds the shear demand associated with this new flexural demand.
key_points: Flexural demand = as-designed Rn (unmodified)
Iterative shear-then-flexure-then-shear check if the design changes
sections.applicability: RC II Option 1 ELR design procedure.

sections.title: RC III Shear and Flexural Requirements
sections.summary: Same procedure as RC II Option 1, but the flexural demand is the POST-Alternate-Path-design nominal flexural strength (since RC III requires AP first).
sections.body: [p. 58] An RC III building must first meet the Alternate Path requirement. The flexural demand for the columns and walls is the nominal flexural strength (Rn) of the design after the Alternate Path requirement is applied and therefore, no design modification is needed to meet the flexural requirement. The shear demand is based on the flexural demand of the component as described above. Apply the procedure in Section 3-3.1.2 to the columns and walls to determine the shear demand. If Equation 3-20 is not satisfied, modify the column or wall design such that adequate design shear strength (Φ Rn) is achieved. If the flexural demand is increased as a result of meeting the shear requirement, check that the design shear strength still exceeds the shear demand associated with this new flexural demand.
key_points: Flexural demand = Rn of the POST-AP design (not the pre-AP baseline)
sections.applicability: RC III ELR design procedure.

sections.title: RC IV Shear and Flexural Requirements
sections.summary: RC IV flexural demand (3-3.5.1) is the larger of a multiplied gravity-only baseline and the all-loads design strength; shear demand (3-3.5.2) follows from that governing flexural demand via the same Section 3-3.1.2 procedure.
sections.body: [p. 58] Heading only in the print; the RC IV requirements are given in Sections 3-3.5.1 (flexural) and 3-3.5.2 (shear).
key_points: RC IV adds a flexural-demand-multiplier step not present in RC II/III
sections.applicability: Overview of the two RC IV ELR sub-sections.

sections.title: RC IV Flexural Requirements
sections.summary: Determine (1) the baseline gravity-only-design Mn after AP, and (2) the all-loads (wind/seismic/gravity) design Mn after AP; flexural demand = max(2.0*baseline, all-loads) for columns, max(1.5*baseline, all-loads) for walls -- redesign if condition 1 (the multiplied baseline) governs.
sections.body: [p. 58] For RC IV, two nominal flexural strengths must first be determined and used to define the flexural demand. First, the baseline nominal flexural strength is determined using the design of the structure when only gravity loads are considered and after the AP procedure is applied. If such a design or analysis was not performed during the initial design and analysis of the new or existing structure, it must be performed to determine the column and load-bearing wall design. [p. 59] Second, the existing nominal flexural strength is determined using the column and load-bearing wall design defined after the Alternate Path procedure was applied to the structural design that incorporated all applied loads (wind, earthquake, gravity, etc). For columns in RC IV structures, the flexural demand is equal to the larger of: 1) the baseline nominal flexural strength multiplied by 2.0 and 2) the nominal flexural strength. If the flexural demand is controlled by condition 1), then redesign the column as required to meet the flexural demand of this controlling condition. For load-bearing walls in RC IV structures, the flexural demand is equal to the larger of 1) the baseline nominal flexural strength multiplied by 1.5, and 2) the nominal flexural strength. If the flexural demand is controlled by condition 1), then redesign the wall as required to meet the flexural demand of this controlling condition.
key_points: Column flexural demand = max(2.0*baseline_gravity_only_Mn, all_loads_Mn)
Wall flexural demand = max(1.5*baseline_gravity_only_Mn, all_loads_Mn)
Redesign triggered when the multiplied baseline governs

equations.description: RC IV column flexural demand = max(2.0*baseline, all-loads Mn)
RC IV wall flexural demand = max(1.5*baseline, all-loads Mn)

sections.applicability: The RC IV flexural-demand calculation, feeding Section 3-3.5.2's shear check.

sections.title: RC IV Shear Requirements
sections.summary: Shear demand is derived from the Section 3-3.5.1 governing flexural demand via the same Section 3-3.1.2 procedure, with the same iterative shear-then-flexure-then-shear re-check.
sections.body: [p. 59] The shear demand for columns and walls is based on the flexural demand as calculated in the above section. Apply the procedure in Section 3-3.1.2 to the columns and walls to determine the shear demand. If Equation 3-20 is not satisfied, modify the column or wall design such that adequate design shear strength (Φ Rn) is achieved. If the flexural demand is increased as a result of meeting the shear requirement, check that the design shear strength still exceeds the shear demand associated with this new flexural demand.
key_points: Same iterative check procedure as RC II Option 1 / RC III, but starting from the RC-IV-multiplied flexural demand
sections.applicability: RC IV ELR shear design.

sections.title: Connection Design for Rebound Reaction Forces
sections.summary: Top/bottom column and wall connections must also resist a REBOUND reaction force equal to 50% of the inbound value, since dynamic loading can push the element in and then rebound it back out.
sections.body: [p. 59] In some dynamic loading scenarios, the column or wall will initially be pushed into the building and then rebound back; the connections must be designed to prevent failure during both phases of loading. Connections at the top and bottom of the columns and walls shall be designed for a rebound reaction force equal to 50% of the inbound value.
key_points: Rebound design force = 0.5 x inbound reaction force

equations.description: Rebound reaction force = 0.5 * inbound reaction force

sections.applicability: Connection design at the top and bottom of every ELR-designed column/wall.

sections.title: Conflicts Between ELR and Other Design Requirements
sections.summary: ELR modifications may be implemented as the designer prefers, but standard building/material codes take precedence over any ELR modification that would violate them.
sections.body: [p. 59] The ELR requirements may be satisfied in a number of ways and as the designer desires, providing the ELR-modified design does not violate the standard building and material-specific design codes. If there is a conflict with the ELR modifications, the building or material-specific design code has precedence and the ELR design must be altered.
key_points: Standard building/material codes always take precedence over an ELR modification
sections.applicability: Conflict-resolution rule when implementing ELR.
